name: Mapping Financial AI to the Rules
title: Mapping Financial AI to the Rules
answer: Mapping financial AI to the rules means taking every AI system used in finance, from credit scoring to fraud detection to customer service, and tying it to the specific laws, regulations, and internal policies that apply. It covers model inventories, control libraries, evidence trails, and the roles that own each step. The work sits inside governance, risk, and financial data security, and it serves auditors, compliance officers, and risk managers. It is not legal advice, but a practical way to show where a system stands against a rule.

sections.body: Mapping financial AI to the rules means taking every AI system used in finance, from credit scoring to fraud detection to customer service, and tying it to the specific laws, regulations, and internal policies that apply. It covers model inventories, control libraries, evidence trails, and the roles that own each step. The work sits inside governance, risk, and financial data security, and it serves auditors, compliance officers, and risk managers. It is not legal advice, but a practical way to show where a system stands against a rule.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The mapping runs on a few core systems: a model registry or inventory, a controls library, a data lineage and provenance store, and a repository for evidence such as test results, approvals, and logs. These sit on cloud or on-premise infrastructure, often connected through APIs to GRC platforms, data catalogs, and ticketing systems. Version control and immutable audit logs matter because a mapping is only useful if you can show what changed, when, and who approved it. The site tracks 732 AI tools, which reflects how many moving parts a typical financial firm may need to account for.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually starts with an inventory of AI use cases, then a risk classification, then a line by line mapping to applicable rules and internal controls. Teams gather evidence, run tests for bias, drift, and security, and record the results in a traceable format. They review the mapping on a schedule and after any material change to the model, the data, or the regulation. The site tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages, which can serve as a reference set when building or updating a mapping.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk come down to data provenance, consent, licensing, and the terms under which a model was built and deployed. Provenance records should show where training data came from, what permissions apply, and how the model was validated. Risk teams look at explainability, bias, security, vendor dependencies, and the ability to audit a third party model. The site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, which illustrate the kinds of disputes that can arise when these areas are left unclear.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward continuous mapping rather than annual reviews, with automated checks that flag when a rule changes or a model drifts. Regulators and standards bodies are converging on common expectations for documentation, testing, and human oversight, which makes reusable control libraries more valuable. As AI-related deals continue, the site tracks 355 merger and acquisition filings, and governance mapping is increasingly part of due diligence. The practical goal is a living record that a firm can defend to an auditor, a regulator, or a court.
